items.stem: What explains why the short-run marginal cost curve eventually rises?
items.answer: Diminishing marginal returns to the variable factor
items.markingKey: Diminishing marginal returns to the variable factor. With a fixed factor, extra workers add less output, so each unit costs more.

items.stem: Distinguish between economies of scale and diminishing marginal returns.
items.answer: Economies of scale are a long-run concept – average costs fall as all inputs increase; diminishing marginal returns are a short-run concept – marginal product falls as a variable factor is added to a fixed one.
items.markingKey: Economies of scale are a long-run concept – average costs fall as all inputs increase; diminishing marginal returns are a short-run concept – marginal product falls as a variable factor is added to a fixed one. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the short-run average total cost curve is U-shaped.
items.answer: Initially AFC falls quickly as fixed costs are spread and AVC falls with increasing returns; later diminishing marginal returns raise AVC and MC, which eventually outweighs the fall in AFC. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Initially AFC falls quickly as fixed costs are spread and AVC falls with increasing returns; later diminishing marginal returns raise AVC and MC, which eventually outweighs the fall in AFC. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which Maersk's Triple-E container ships shows technical economies of scale.
items.answer: Ships carrying around 18,000 containers cut fuel and crew costs per container substantially compared with smaller vessels. Larger ships spread fixed crew and fuel costs over more units, lowering the long-run average cost of shipping each container.
items.markingKey: Context (Ships carrying around 18,000 containers cut fuel and crew costs per container substantially compared with smaller vessels.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Larger ships spread fixed crew and fuel costs over more units, lowering the long-run average cost of shipping each container. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to technical economies of scale.

items.answer: Ships carrying around 18,000 containers cut fuel and crew costs per container substantially compared with smaller vessels. Larger ships spread fixed crew and fuel costs over more units, lowering the long-run average cost of shipping each container.

items.stem: Identify two economies of scale a firm such as Toyota might benefit from.
items.answer: e.g. technical (large automated assembly lines), purchasing (bulk discounts on steel and parts), financial (borrowing at lower interest rates), marketing (advertising spread over many cars).
items.markingKey: e.g. technical (large automated assembly lines), purchasing (bulk discounts on steel and parts), financial (borrowing at lower interest rates), marketing (advertising spread over many cars).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Firms should always aim to grow to benefit from economies of scale.
items.answer: Growth is beneficial up to the minimum efficient scale; beyond that diseconomies and market size limit its benefits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lower average costs and prices; greater market power and financial strength. Arguments against: diseconomies of scale beyond the minimum efficient scale; growth may reduce flexibility; demand may be too small for large scale. Supported judgement: Growth is beneficial up to the minimum efficient scale; beyond that diseconomies and market size limit its benefits.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that Economies of scale mean that large firms are always more efficient than small firms?
items.answer: Large firms can be more efficient up to a point, but beyond the minimum efficient scale diseconomies arise and in many industries small firms are efficient.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lower average costs through specialisation, bulk buying, cheaper finance; can invest in R&D. Arguments against: diseconomies of scale beyond the minimum efficient scale; small firms can be flexible and innovative; in some industries (hairdressing) the efficient scale is small. Supported judgement: Large firms can be more efficient up to a point, but beyond the minimum efficient scale diseconomies arise and in many industries small firms are efficient. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Costs that change with output, such as raw materials and hourly wages"?
items.answer: variable costs
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of variable costs.

items.stem: Explain why the long-run average cost curve is often U-shaped.
items.answer: At first, economies of scale (specialisation, bulk buying, technical, financial) lower average costs as the firm grows; beyond the minimum efficient scale, diseconomies of scale (coordination, communication, motivation problems) raise average costs.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: At first, economies of scale (specialisation, bulk buying, technical, financial) lower average costs as the firm grows; beyond the minimum efficient scale, diseconomies of scale (coordination, communication, motivation problems) raise average costs. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that Fixed costs never change. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Fixed costs do not vary with output in the short run, but they can change over time (e.g. a rent increase) and in the long run all costs are variable.
items.markingKey: Fixed costs do not vary with output in the short run, but they can change over time (e.g. a rent increase) and in the long run all costs are variable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the shape of the long-run average cost curve with reference to economies and diseconomies of scale.
items.answer: Diagram: cost on the vertical axis, output on the horizontal; U-shaped LRAC as the envelope of several SRAC curves. Falling section: economies of scale; minimum point: minimum efficient scale; rising section: diseconomies of scale.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: cost on the vertical axis, output on the horizontal; U-shaped LRAC as the envelope of several SRAC curves. Falling section: economies of scale; minimum point: minimum efficient scale; rising section: diseconomies of scale. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Perfectly competitive firms in long-run equilibrium are both allocatively and productively efficient because of which condition?
options: P = MC and P = minimum ATC
items.answer: P = MC and P = minimum ATC
items.markingKey: B. Price equals marginal cost and output is at minimum average cost.

items.stem: A student claims that Firms should always shut down when they make a loss. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: In the short run a firm should continue if price covers AVC, because shutting down still leaves fixed costs to pay; it shuts down only if P < AVC (and leaves in the long run if P < ATC).
items.markingKey: In the short run a firm should continue if price covers AVC, because shutting down still leaves fixed costs to pay; it shuts down only if P < AVC (and leaves in the long run if P < ATC). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A small coffee farm in Vietnam sells in a perfectly competitive market at a price of $30 per unit. Its total costs are: Q = 0: TC = 100, Q = 1: TC = 108, Q = 2: TC = 124, Q = 3: TC = 143, Q = 4: TC = 168, Q = 5: TC = 201, Q = 6: TC = 239. Using MC = MR, find the profit-maximising output and calculate the profit or loss.
With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the short-run equilibrium of a perfectly competitive firm making abnormal profits.
items.answer: Two diagrams: industry D and S set market price Pm; firm faces horizontal D = AR = MR at Pm. Firm produces Q where MC = MR; ATC at Q is below Pm; abnormal profit = (Pm − ATC) × Q shaded. In the long run entry lowers price to minimum ATC.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Two diagrams: industry D and S set market price Pm; firm faces horizontal D = AR = MR at Pm. Firm produces Q where MC = MR; ATC at Q is below Pm; abnormal profit = (Pm − ATC) × Q shaded. In the long run entry lowers price to minimum ATC. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Explain why the agricultural market for wheat is often used as an example close to perfect competition.
items.answer: Many small farmers, a homogeneous product, buyers well informed about prices (world markets), and relatively free entry and exit; each farmer accepts the market price.
items.markingKey: Many small farmers, a homogeneous product, buyers well informed about prices (world markets), and relatively free entry and exit; each farmer accepts the market price.

items.stem: Using diagrams, explain how a perfectly competitive industry adjusts from short-run abnormal profits to long-run equilibrium.
items.answer: Firm diagram: P1 above ATC at MC = MR, abnormal profit rectangle; industry diagram: new firms enter, supply shifts right, price falls to P2 = minimum ATC; firm earns normal profit at MC = MR = AR = ATC.
items.markingKey: Firm diagram: P1 above ATC at MC = MR, abnormal profit rectangle; industry diagram: new firms enter, supply shifts right, price falls to P2 = minimum ATC; firm earns normal profit at MC = MR = AR = ATC.

items.stem: "Perfect competition is the ideal market structure." Discuss.
items.answer: Perfect competition is an efficiency benchmark, but dynamic efficiency, economies of scale and product variety mean other structures can deliver benefits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: allocative and productive efficiency in the long run; low prices and consumer sovereignty; no abnormal profits. Arguments against: no abnormal profits to fund R&D, so less dynamic efficiency; no economies of scale; homogeneous products limit consumer choice; the model is unrealistic. Supported judgement: Perfect competition is an efficiency benchmark, but dynamic efficiency, economies of scale and product variety mean other structures can deliver benefits. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "perfect competition"?
options: The study of strategic decision-making where the outcome for each player depends on the choices of others
Costs that change with output, such as raw materials and hourly wages
A market structure with many small firms, identical products, perfect information and free entry and exit, so each firm is a price taker
Total cost divided by quantity of output, equal to AFC + AVC
items.answer: A market structure with many small firms, identical products, perfect information and free entry and exit, so each firm is a price taker
items.markingKey: C. "perfect competition" is a market structure with many small firms, identical products, perfect information and free entry and exit, so each firm is a price taker.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the shut-down price and the break-even price.
items.answer: The shut-down price equals minimum AVC – below it the firm should stop producing in the short run; the break-even price equals minimum ATC – at it the firm makes normal profit.
items.markingKey: The shut-down price equals minimum AVC – below it the firm should stop producing in the short run; the break-even price equals minimum ATC – at it the firm makes normal profit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the market for foreign exchange as an example, explain features of perfect competition.
items.answer: Huge numbers of buyers and sellers trade identical currencies with near-perfect information and prices that adjust instantly. No individual trader can influence the price; they are price takers in a highly competitive market.
items.markingKey: Context (Huge numbers of buyers and sellers trade identical currencies with near-perfect information and prices that adjust instantly.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: No individual trader can influence the price; they are price takers in a highly competitive market. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to features of perfect competition.

items.stem: A profit-maximising monopolist produces where which of the following holds?
items.answer: MC = MR
items.markingKey: C. It then charges the price on the demand (AR) curve at that output.

items.stem: Briefly explain why monopolies might benefit consumers.
items.answer: Abnormal profits can fund research and development (dynamic efficiency), and large economies of scale can mean lower costs and possibly lower prices than a fragmented industry (natural monopoly).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Abnormal profits can fund research and development (dynamic efficiency), and large economies of scale can mean lower costs and possibly lower prices than a fragmented industry (natural monopoly). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Natural monopolies should always be broken up into smaller competing firms." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Breaking up a natural monopoly would raise average costs because economies of scale are lost; regulation or public ownership is usually preferred.
items.markingKey: Breaking up a natural monopoly would raise average costs because economies of scale are lost; regulation or public ownership is usually preferred. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: De Beers controlled most of the world's rough diamond supply for much of the 20th century. Identify the barrier to entry and explain how it allowed high prices.
items.answer: Control of essential resources (mines) and stockpiling; by limiting supply De Beers kept prices well above marginal cost, earning abnormal profit.
items.markingKey: Control of essential resources (mines) and stockpiling; by limiting supply De Beers kept prices well above marginal cost, earning abnormal profit.

items.stem: Explain, with the help of a fully labelled diagram, why a natural monopoly exists and the problem with regulating it using marginal cost pricing.
items.answer: Diagram: falling LRAC over the whole range of market demand; MC below AC; demand AR and MR. Unregulated: MC = MR, Pm > AC, abnormal profit. Marginal cost pricing (P = MC) gives allocative efficiency but P < AC, a loss requiring subsidy; average cost pricing (P = AC) gives normal profit with output below the allocatively efficient level.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: falling LRAC over the whole range of market demand; MC below AC; demand AR and MR. Unregulated: MC = MR, Pm > AC, abnormal profit. Marginal cost pricing (P = MC) gives allocative efficiency but P < AC, a loss requiring subsidy; average cost pricing (P = AC) gives normal profit with output below the allocatively efficient level. items.stem: Using a diagram, compare the price and output of a profit-maximising monopolist with those of a perfectly competitive industry with the same costs, and explain the welfare loss.
items.answer: Monopolist: MC = MR, Qm, Pm on AR. Competitive industry: P = MC, Qc > Qm, Pc < Pm. Welfare loss triangle between AR and MC from Qm to Qc; consumer surplus transferred to the monopolist as abnormal profit.
items.markingKey: Monopolist: MC = MR, Qm, Pm on AR. Competitive industry: P = MC, Qc > Qm, Pc < Pm. Welfare loss triangle between AR and MC from Qm to Qc; consumer surplus transferred to the monopolist as abnormal profit.

items.stem: "Monopolies are always against the public interest." Discuss.
items.answer: Monopolies impose static efficiency costs, but where economies of scale or innovation are important, regulated monopolies can serve the public interest.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher prices and lower output than competition; allocative and possibly productive inefficiency; x-inefficiency from lack of competition. Arguments against: economies of scale (natural monopoly); abnormal profits fund R&D and innovation (pharmaceuticals, technology); regulation can limit abuse. items.stem: Briefly explain why regulating a natural monopoly by setting price equal to marginal cost would cause losses.
items.answer: In a natural monopoly ATC is falling over the relevant range, so MC lies below ATC; a price equal to MC is below ATC and the firm makes a loss, requiring a subsidy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In a natural monopoly ATC is falling over the relevant range, so MC lies below ATC; a price equal to MC is below ATC and the firm makes a loss, requiring a subsidy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why a monopoly is allocatively inefficient.
items.answer: It produces where MC = MR; because MR is below price, price is above MC at that output (P > MC), so consumers value extra units more than they cost, but they are not produced – a welfare loss.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It produces where MC = MR; because MR is below price, price is above MC at that output (P > MC), so consumers value extra units more than they cost, but they are not produced – a welfare loss. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to the patent on Gilead's hepatitis C drug sofosbuvir (Sovaldi), explain how it illustrates monopoly power from legal barriers.
items.answer: Launched in the US in 2013 at about $84,000 for a 12-week course, far above production cost; generic versions in India later cost a few hundred dollars. The patent created a legal monopoly, allowing price far above marginal cost while funding R&D – the trade-off between static and dynamic efficiency.
items.markingKey: Context (Launched in the US in 2013 at about $84,000 for a 12-week course, far above production cost; generic versions in India later cost a few hundred dollars.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "collusion"?
options: Obstacles that prevent new firms from entering a market, such as economies of scale, legal barriers (patents, licences), control of resources and brand loyalty
Cooperation between firms to limit competition, for example by fixing prices or sharing markets; formal collusion is a cartel
Falls in long-run average cost as a firm increases the scale of all its inputs
A firm maximises profit by producing the output at which marginal cost equals marginal revenue (MC = MR), with MC rising
items.answer: Cooperation between firms to limit competition, for example by fixing prices or sharing markets; formal collusion is a cartel
items.markingKey: B. "collusion" is cooperation between firms to limit competition, for example by fixing prices or sharing markets; formal collusion is a cartel.

items.stem: Explain why firms in oligopoly may prefer non-price competition.
items.answer: If one firm cuts price, rivals are likely to match it, starting a price war that reduces all firms' profits; competing through advertising, branding and product innovation avoids this while still gaining market share.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If one firm cuts price, rivals are likely to match it, starting a price war that reduces all firms' profits; competing through advertising, branding and product innovation avoids this while still gaining market share. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how price discrimination can increase a firm's profit.
items.answer: By charging higher prices to consumers with inelastic demand and lower prices to those with elastic demand, the firm converts consumer surplus into revenue and sells to customers who would not pay a single high price.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: By charging higher prices to consumers with inelastic demand and lower prices to those with elastic demand, the firm converts consumer surplus into revenue and sells to customers who would not pay a single high price. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Supermarket 1 and Supermarket 2 are the only two firms in a market. Profits ($m) for (Supermarket 1, Supermarket 2): both choose "Maintain fare": (58, 58); Supermarket 1 "Cut fare", Supermarket 2 "Maintain fare": (75, 25); Supermarket 1 "Maintain fare", Supermarket 2 "Cut fare": (25, 75); both "Cut fare": (43, 43). Identify each firm's dominant strategy, the likely outcome and explain why the firms might try to collude.
items.answer: Dominant strategy for both: "Cut fare"; outcome (43, 43); collusion on "Maintain fare" would give (58, 58)
items.markingKey: If rival chooses "Maintain fare": 75 > 58; if rival chooses "Cut fare": 43 > 25 ⇒ "Cut fare" dominant [2]; Nash equilibrium (43, 43) [1]; joint profit higher at (58, 58), so incentive to collude, but each has an incentive to cheat – prisoner's dilemma [1].

items.stem: A student claims that in oligopoly firms always collude because it maximises their profits. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Collusion is usually illegal and unstable; firms face incentives to cheat, and many oligopolies compete fiercely on price or through non-price competition.
items.markingKey: Collusion is usually illegal and unstable; firms face incentives to cheat, and many oligopolies compete fiercely on price or through non-price competition. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using a payoff matrix, explain why firms in oligopoly may have an incentive to collude and an incentive to cheat on any agreement.
items.answer: Matrix with high/low price strategies; joint profit is highest if both price high (collusion); each firm gains by undercutting (cheating) if the other keeps price high; dominant strategy leads to low-price equilibrium; repeated games, trust and enforcement explain collusion; legal penalties.
items.markingKey: Matrix with high/low price strategies; joint profit is highest if both price high (collusion); each firm gains by undercutting (cheating) if the other keeps price high; dominant strategy leads to low-price equilibrium; repeated games, trust and enforcement explain collusion; legal penalties.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "price discrimination".
items.answer: Charging different prices to different consumers for the same product for reasons not related to differences in cost
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: charging different prices to different consumers for the same product for reasons not related to differences in cost. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between monopolistic competition and oligopoly.
items.answer: Monopolistic competition has many firms with differentiated products and low barriers, so long-run profits are normal; oligopoly has a few interdependent firms and high barriers, so abnormal profits can persist.
items.markingKey: Monopolistic competition has many firms with differentiated products and low barriers, so long-run profits are normal; oligopoly has a few interdependent firms and high barriers, so abnormal profits can persist. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how airlines practise price discrimination, and why business travellers usually pay more.
items.answer: Airlines charge different fares for the same seat according to booking time, flexibility and day of travel; business travellers have inelastic demand (urgent, employer pays), so they are charged higher fares, while leisure travellers with elastic demand get cheap advance fares.
items.markingKey: Airlines charge different fares for the same seat according to booking time, flexibility and day of travel; business travellers have inelastic demand (urgent, employer pays), so they are charged higher fares, while leisure travellers with elastic demand get cheap advance fares.

items.stem: Zara writes: "Price discrimination means charging different prices because some customers cost more to serve." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Price discrimination is charging different prices for the same product for reasons not related to cost differences, based on differences in willingness to pay (PED).
items.markingKey: Price discrimination is charging different prices for the same product for reasons not related to cost differences, based on differences in willingness to pay (PED). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that if marginal cost is rising, average total cost must also be rising. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: ATC rises only when MC is above ATC; MC can be rising while still below ATC, in which case ATC is still falling.
items.markingKey: ATC rises only when MC is above ATC; MC can be rising while still below ATC, in which case ATC is still falling. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a firm maximises profit where MC = MR.
items.answer: If MR > MC, producing an extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost, so profit rises; if MC > MR, the last unit reduces profit. Profit is greatest where the two are equal.

items.stem: The demand for a patented medicine is P = 68 − 4Q, so MR = 68 − 8Q. Marginal cost is constant at $20. Calculate the profit-maximising price and output, the firm's profit, and the welfare loss compared with a competitive outcome where P = MC.
items.answer: Q = 6, P = $44; profit = $144; welfare loss = $72

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Two supermarket chains dominate a country's grocery market. If both keep prices high, each earns $50m profit. If one cuts prices and the other does not, the price-cutter earns $70m and the other $20m. If both cut prices, each earns $35m.
— Hypothetical payoff data

Using game theory, explain the likely outcome and why it is a dilemma for the firms.
items.answer: Whatever the rival does, cutting price gives more profit (70 > 50; 35 > 20), so cutting is a dominant strategy; both cut and earn $35m each, although both keeping prices high would give $50m each – a prisoner's dilemma.
items.markingKey: Whatever the rival does, cutting price gives more profit (70 > 50; 35 > 20), so cutting is a dominant strategy; both cut and earn $35m each, although both keeping prices high would give $50m each – a prisoner's dilemma. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: The total cost of a small brewery is: Q = 0: TC = 80, Q = 1: TC = 97, Q = 2: TC = 109, Q = 3: TC = 126, Q = 4: TC = 149, Q = 5: TC = 181 (costs in $). State the fixed cost and calculate AFC, AVC, ATC and MC at Q = 4.
Draw a diagram to illustrate the short-run equilibrium of a perfectly competitive firm making abnormal profits, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Two diagrams: industry D and S set market price Pm; firm faces horizontal D = AR = MR at Pm. Firm produces Q where MC = MR; ATC at Q is below Pm; abnormal profit = (Pm − ATC) × Q shaded. In the long run entry lowers price to minimum ATC.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Two diagrams: industry D and S set market price Pm; firm faces horizontal D = AR = MR at Pm. Firm produces Q where MC = MR; ATC at Q is below Pm; abnormal profit = (Pm − ATC) × Q shaded. In the long run entry lowers price to minimum ATC. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

A regulator sets a price cap of RPI − 3% on a national water company, meaning prices may rise by 3 percentage points less than inflation each year. The company says the cap will make investment in new pipes difficult; consumer groups say it makes abnormal profits.
— Hypothetical regulator statement

Using the extract, explain why the regulator uses a price cap for a natural monopoly.
items.answer: A natural monopoly would otherwise set P > MC and earn abnormal profit; the cap limits price increases, forcing efficiency gains (X = 3%) and passing them to consumers, while still letting the firm cover costs; risk of under-investment.
items.markingKey: A natural monopoly would otherwise set P > MC and earn abnormal profit; the cap limits price increases, forcing efficiency gains (X = 3%) and passing them to consumers, while still letting the firm cover costs; risk of under-investment. items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate third-degree price discrimination between two groups of consumers, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagrams for market A (inelastic demand) and market B (elastic demand) with a common MC. The firm sets MR = MC in each market: a higher price in A and a lower price in B. Total profit is higher than with a single price because consumer surplus is captured in market A while sales are expanded in market B.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagrams for market A (inelastic demand) and market B (elastic demand) with a common MC. The firm sets MR = MC in each market: a higher price in A and a lower price in B. items.stem: A bakery has fixed costs of $200 per day and variable costs that rise as output increases. Explain the shapes of its AFC, AVC, ATC and MC curves in the short run.
items.answer: AFC falls continuously (fixed cost spread); AVC and MC fall then rise (increasing then diminishing returns); MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minima; the gap between ATC and AVC equals AFC and narrows as output rises.
items.markingKey: AFC falls continuously (fixed cost spread); AVC and MC fall then rise (increasing then diminishing returns); MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minima; the gap between ATC and AVC equals AFC and narrows as output rises.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that the model of perfect competition has no relevance to real-world markets.
items.answer: Perfect competition is rarely observed exactly, but it remains a useful benchmark and approximates some markets.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: assumptions (perfect information, identical products) rarely hold. Arguments against: some markets come close (agriculture, foreign exchange); provides an efficiency benchmark for policy; explains entry and exit and competitive pressure. Judgement: Perfect competition is rarely observed exactly, but it remains a useful benchmark and approximates some markets. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that monopolies are always against the public interest.
items.answer: Monopolies impose static efficiency costs, but where economies of scale or innovation are important, regulated monopolies can serve the public interest.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher prices and lower output than competition; allocative and possibly productive inefficiency; x-inefficiency from lack of competition. items.stem: "Price discrimination always makes consumers worse off." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Price discrimination redistributes surplus to firms but can increase output and access for some groups, so its effect on consumers is mixed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: transfers consumer surplus to producers; consumers in the high-price market pay more. Arguments against: consumers in low-price markets (students, off-peak) may gain access they would otherwise not have; can make services viable that would otherwise not be supplied (rural rail, medicines); output may rise towards the efficient level. Supported judgement: Price discrimination redistributes surplus to firms but can increase output and access for some groups, so its effect on consumers is mixed. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "variable costs"?
options: Rises in long-run average cost as a firm grows beyond its optimum size, for example because of coordination problems
Costs that do not change with output in the short run, such as rent and insurance
Costs that change with output, such as raw materials and hourly wages
A market structure with many firms selling differentiated products, low barriers to entry and some control over price
items.answer: Costs that change with output, such as raw materials and hourly wages
items.markingKey: C. "variable costs" is costs that change with output, such as raw materials and hourly wages.

items.stem: In the long run in perfect competition, firms earn which of the following?
items.answer: Normal profit only
items.markingKey: A. Free entry and exit remove abnormal profits and losses.

items.stem: A monopolist operates on which part of its demand curve?
items.answer: The price elastic part, where MR > 0
items.markingKey: The price elastic part, where MR > 0. MC > 0 = MR requires MR positive, i.e. elastic demand.

items.stem: Distinguish between formal collusion and tacit collusion.
items.answer: Formal collusion is an explicit agreement between firms (a cartel), usually illegal; tacit collusion is coordination without an agreement, such as price leadership, where firms follow a dominant firm's prices.
items.markingKey: Formal collusion is an explicit agreement between firms (a cartel), usually illegal; tacit collusion is coordination without an agreement, such as price leadership, where firms follow a dominant firm's prices. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between variable costs and fixed costs.
items.answer: Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run (rent); variable costs rise with output (raw materials).
items.markingKey: Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run (rent); variable costs rise with output (raw materials). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how abnormal profits are eliminated in perfect competition in the long run.
items.answer: Abnormal profits attract new firms (free entry, perfect information); market supply shifts right, the price falls until P = minimum ATC and only normal profit is made.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Abnormal profits attract new firms (free entry, perfect information); market supply shifts right, the price falls until P = minimum ATC and only normal profit is made. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between perfect competition and monopoly.
items.answer: A monopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand curve, sets P > MC and can earn long-run abnormal profit behind barriers; perfectly competitive firms are price takers that earn normal profit in the long run with P = MC = minimum ATC.
items.markingKey: A monopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand curve, sets P > MC and can earn long-run abnormal profit behind barriers; perfectly competitive firms are price takers that earn normal profit in the long run with P = MC = minimum ATC. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run (rent); variable costs rise with output (raw materials).

items.stem: "A perfectly competitive firm can raise its price above the market price to increase profit." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It is a price taker: identical products and perfect information mean that if it raises price, customers buy from rivals and its sales fall to zero.
items.markingKey: It is a price taker: identical products and perfect information mean that if it raises price, customers buy from rivals and its sales fall to zero. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline why a natural monopoly exists and the problem with regulating it using marginal cost pricing.
items.answer: Diagram: falling LRAC over the whole range of market demand; MC below AC; demand AR and MR. Unregulated: MC = MR, Pm > AC, abnormal profit. Marginal cost pricing (P = MC) gives allocative efficiency but P < AC, a loss requiring subsidy; average cost pricing (P = AC) gives normal profit with output below the allocatively efficient level.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: falling LRAC over the whole range of market demand; MC below AC; demand AR and MR. Unregulated: MC = MR, Pm > AC, abnormal profit. Marginal cost pricing (P = MC) gives allocative efficiency but P < AC, a loss requiring subsidy; average cost pricing (P = AC) gives normal profit with output below the allocatively efficient level. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the long-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition.
items.answer: Diagram: downward-sloping AR and MR; MC and ATC. Firm produces where MC = MR; in the long run entry shifts AR left until it is tangent to ATC, so P = ATC and profit is normal; output is to the left of minimum ATC (excess capacity) and P > MC (allocative inefficiency).
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: downward-sloping AR and MR; MC and ATC. Firm produces where MC = MR; in the long run entry shifts AR left until it is tangent to ATC, so P = ATC and profit is normal; output is to the left of minimum ATC (excess capacity) and P > MC (allocative inefficiency). Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Ana writes: "If marginal cost is rising, average total cost must also be rising." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: ATC rises only when MC is above ATC; MC can be rising while still below ATC, in which case ATC is still falling.
items.markingKey: ATC rises only when MC is above ATC; MC can be rising while still below ATC, in which case ATC is still falling. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the market for foreign exchange and explain what it reveals about features of perfect competition.
items.answer: Huge numbers of buyers and sellers trade identical currencies with near-perfect information and prices that adjust instantly. No individual trader can influence the price; they are price takers in a highly competitive market.
items.markingKey: Context (Huge numbers of buyers and sellers trade identical currencies with near-perfect information and prices that adjust instantly.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: No individual trader can influence the price; they are price takers in a highly competitive market. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to features of perfect competition.

items.stem: A student claims that a monopolist can charge any price it likes and still sell as much as it wants. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A monopolist faces the market demand curve: a higher price reduces quantity demanded, so it chooses price and quantity together to maximise profit.
items.markingKey: A monopolist faces the market demand curve: a higher price reduces quantity demanded, so it chooses price and quantity together to maximise profit. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which OPEC+ production cuts in 2016 and 2020 shows collusion in oligopoly.
items.answer: In April 2020 OPEC+ agreed to cut output by almost 10 million barrels a day as demand collapsed during the pandemic. Members acted together to restrict supply and support prices, behaving like a monopoly, though compliance with quotas varied.
items.markingKey: Context (In April 2020 OPEC+ agreed to cut output by almost 10 million barrels a day as demand collapsed during the pandemic.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Members acted together to restrict supply and support prices, behaving like a monopoly, though compliance with quotas varied. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to collusion in oligopoly.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Firms should always aim to grow to benefit from economies of scale."
items.answer: Growth is beneficial up to the minimum efficient scale; beyond that diseconomies and market size limit its benefits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lower average costs and prices; greater market power and financial strength. Arguments against: diseconomies of scale beyond the minimum efficient scale; growth may reduce flexibility; demand may be too small for large scale. Supported judgement: Growth is beneficial up to the minimum efficient scale; beyond that diseconomies and market size limit its benefits.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that natural monopolies should be owned by the government.
items.answer: Either public ownership or regulated private ownership can work; the choice depends on governance quality and regulatory capacity.

items.stem: "Oligopolies are harmful to consumers." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Oligopolies can harm consumers when they collude, but competitive oligopolies often deliver low prices and innovation; outcomes depend on behaviour and regulation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: tendency to collude (cartels, tacit price leadership) raising prices; high barriers protect abnormal profits; allocative inefficiency.
